talks.title: Recon2023-EVM- SamshingVirtualFunctionPointersOnTheHeightsOfMountElbrus
talks.teaser: Explores recon2023-EVM- SamshingVirtualFunctionPointersOnTheHeightsOfMountElbrus and evaluates key implications for security practitioners.
talks.summary:
Overview: EVM (Azie) presents at RECON on reverse engineering the Russian Elbrus processor architecture, exploring indigenous CPU design through technically dense disassembly analysis.

Key Topics: Elbrus architecture named after Russia's highest mountain; indigenous processor development history and military procurement claims; virtual function pointer smashing techniques; and embedded reverse engineering methodology.

Technical Details: EVM walks through Elbrus disassembly with code available on GitHub, examining virtual function pointer exploitation on the architecture. She contextualizes hype around Russian processor independence versus actual military deployment.

Takeaways: Indigenous processor architectures present unique reverse engineering challenges. Security researchers should examine non-x86 platforms as nations pursue technology sovereignty.

talks.title: Maxime Rossi and Damiano Melotti - Dissecting the Modern Android Data Encryption Scheme
talks.teaser: Details maxime Rossi and Damiano Melotti - Dissecting the Modern Android Data Encryption Scheme and evaluates key implications for security practitioners.
talks.summary:
Research Motivation

Researchers Maxime Rossi and Damiano Melotti of quarex lab explain Android data encryption at rest, triggered by a Pixel Titanium chip inquiry after water damage killed the main SoC but left the secure element alive—they could not recover data and sought to map why the application processor remains essential.

Encryption Architecture

Android encrypts files per-object with keys derived from a master key; metadata uses separate protection. Features like Direct Boot and multi-user support rely on per-file keys. Keys may live in TEE Keymaster or StrongBox hardware, with raw key material never leaving protected environments.

Software-Only Attack Models

They present two proof-of-concept software attacks assuming plentiful bugs—no hardware or crypto breaks—exploring how authentication gates access to credential-encrypted keys and application IDs. The talk clarifies that successful decryption requires authenticated user credentials even when secure elements survive, defining the trust boundary defenders must protect.

talks.title: Simon Scannell Remotely Exploiting An Antivirus Engine
talks.teaser: Examines simon Scannell Remotely Exploiting An Antivirus Engine and evaluates key implications for security practitioners.
talks.summary:
ClamAV Attack Surface

Google Cloud researcher Simon Scannell targets ClamAV, the widely deployed open-source AV scanning emails, web uploads, Zimbra, Cisco secure web appliances, and cloud storage pipelines. Written in C, it recursively unpacks archives and dispatches format-specific parsers—many complex (HFS+, DMG, cpio)—expanding untrusted input reach.

Non-Interactive Exploitation Constraints

ClamAV is not a conversational protocol; attackers typically learn only scan pass/fail via intermediaries. Full ASLR, multithreaded clamd restarts on segfault after signature reload delays, blocking classic info-leak-then-ROP chains, partial overwrites, data-only heap corruption, or brute-force ASLR.

CVE-2023-20032 HFS+ Overflow

A missing bounds check lets attacker-controlled HFS+ volume read_size trigger a powerful heap overflow (4KB–2MB) during Apple filesystem parsing—remotely triggerable in default configs (CVSS 9.8). Nesting malicious inner formats inside allowed containers bypasses upload filters.

Exploitation Strategy and Case Study

Despite constraints, Scannell details novel approaches to achieve impact without pointer leaks, culminating in an authenticated remote code execution case study on an email server—turning the defender into the attacked component.

talks.title: Travis Goodspeed Recent Experiments with Mask ROMs
talks.teaser: Demonstrates travis Goodspeed Recent Experiments with Mask ROMs and evaluates key implications for security practitioners.
talks.summary:
Clipper Chip context

Travis Goodspeed revisits the third-generation Fortezza Clipper card: U.S. government key-escrow cryptography using Skipjack, sold only in hardware to limit reverse engineering. Prior work by Matt Blaze covered driver interfaces, weak 16-bit checksum validation, and family-key attacks.

Mask ROM basics

Unlike flash or EEPROM, mask ROM is factory-programmed and identical across production runs, often used for bootloaders or copy protection. Reading it requires decapping, delayering, and sometimes staining because bits may be buried and chemically ambiguous over time.

Photography workflow

He shows a classified Skipjack S-box lookup table imaged as blue ones on a bit grid. His CAD tool marks row/column lines rather than every bit, reducing manual labor; software then extracts ones and zeros, sometimes requiring inversion after chemical processing.

Existing toolchain

Public extractors include Rampart and BitRacked; logical reordering tools include John McMaster's Zorom solver and Chris Gerlinski's Bit Viewer. Goodspeed introduces a new extractor for the photography step and hopes to improve byte-order conversion next.
